direct_answer: Yes. Shell discloses that its “climate change transition plans are delivered through our strategy”, supported by processes and GHG emission reduction targets/ambition, with the aim of becoming “a net-zero emissions energy business by 2050” [Source 1]. Shell also states it supports the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal and describes how it derived its net carbon intensity (NCI) targets from IPCC AR6 1.5°C scenarios (including excluding scenarios overly reliant on removals/bioenergy, removing outliers, and constructing a 1.5°C pathway), concluding it believes these targets are aligned with 1.5°C [Source 12]. Shell further states its oil products (Scope 3 Category 11) ambition (15–20% reduction by 2030 vs 2021) is “compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5 C” based on the same AR6 1.5°C scenario set [Source 12]. Therefore, Shell indicates it has a transition plan and asserts alignment/compatibility with limiting warming to 1.5°C (via its targets/ambition and methodology) [Source 1][Source 12]. No timeline for adopting a plan is applicable because Shell indicates a plan exists [Source 1].
compliance_rationale: Evidence shows the undertaking has a transition plan (embedded in strategy) and provides an explanation of 1.5°C alignment/compatibility for key targets (NCI targets and oil products Scope 3 ambition) including the methodology (derived from IPCC AR6 1.5°C scenarios and how scenarios were filtered/processed) [Source 1][Source 12]. However, the retrieved passages do not provide full ESRS E1-4 elements (e.g., whether targets are science-based under a recognised framework, external assurance status) and do not comprehensively evidence that the entire transition plan (beyond selected targets) is aligned with 1.5°C [Source 12].
disclosure_gaps: Explicit statement that the overall transition plan (not only specific targets) is aligned with limiting warming to 1.5°C, with clear linkage across all material emissions scopes and levers (beyond NCI and oil products ambition) (insufficient evidence in retrieved passages) [Source 1][Source 12].
Whether Shell’s GHG targets are “science-based” under a recognised framework/initiative (e.g., SBTi) (not evidenced in retrieved passages) [Source 12].
Underlying climate and policy scenarios used for targets beyond the described AR6 1.5°C scenario approach (e.g., specific scenario names/assumptions) (not fully evidenced) [Source 12].
Whether and which targets have been externally assured (not evidenced in retrieved passages).

Clear ESRS-boundary-consistent target definitions and reconciliation where targets “predate the CSRD and differ from the ESRS boundary and definitions” (gap noted but not resolved in retrieved passages) [Source 12].
key_findings: Shell reports it has climate change transition plans delivered through its strategy, supported by processes and GHG reduction targets/ambition, aiming for net-zero emissions energy business by 2050 [Source 1].

Shell states support for the Paris Agreement 1.5°C goal and claims its NCI targets are aligned with 1.5°C, describing a methodology based on IPCC AR6 1.5°C scenarios (filtering scenarios and constructing a pathway) [Source 12].
Shell claims its oil products Scope 3 Category 11 ambition (15–20% reduction by 2030 vs 2021) is compatible with limiting warming to 1.5°C using the same AR6 1.5°C scenario set [Source 12].
